changelog.change: Registered the word-search set: the anagram's serving gates with the length floor at 4, the same floor the missing-letters set uses.
changelog.why: Row 20 - the gates are the anagram's unchanged for the fourth time, because what makes a word fair to be ASKED for does not depend on how it is asked. Only the floor moves, and it moves for a reason particular to a grid: a 4-ezhuthu word covers four cells, and an 8x8 grid holds 512 straight runs of that length in its eight directions, so a short word is nearly as likely to turn up in the filler as it is to be placed on purpose. Measured over 300 generated boards, scanning for served words of 4 to 6 ezhuthu finds an unintended one on 74.2 percent of grids, and dropping the scan to 5 and 6 ezhuthu drops that to 7.7 - so almost every accidental hit is a short word. The floor of 4 is kept rather than raised to 5 because an unintended word is RECORDED and answered, not refused (the anagram's anagramFanOut precedent), and because 6,160 of the 25,210 four-plus rows are 6 ezhuthu: raising the floor would throw away the length that packs a grid loosest. The ceiling stays at 6 because a 7-ezhuthu word leaves one spare cell on an 8-wide board, so it can only ever be placed along a full row, column or main diagonal, which a player learns to look for once and then never searches for again. wordClasses stays headword alone on the same terms as the other three sets.

changelog.change: Registered the wordle set: the anagram's serving gates with the length pinned to exactly 6 ezhuthu.
changelog.why: Row 19 - the gates are the anagram's unchanged, for the third time, because what makes a word fair to be ASKED for does not depend on how it is asked. The length is the whole decision, and it went the opposite way to the plan's guess of 5. In English a longer answer is harder; in Tamil it is measurably EASIER, because the alphabet is 247 ezhuthu rather than 26 letters and stays effectively constant across lengths - 203 to 217 distinct ezhuthu are in play at every length - so an extra position is an extra constraint against a near-fixed alphabet rather than an extra degree of freedom. Simulated against a player who guesses a familiar word still consistent with every mark, the median solve is 15 guesses at 3 ezhuthu, 10 at 4, 7 at 5 and 5 at 6. A 5-ezhuthu board - the roadmap's suggestion - is lost more often than it is won at any sane attempt budget, and a 3-ezhuthu one is not a game. 6 is also the CEILING as well as the floor: a wordle's keyboard readout and its shareable grid both assume one fixed width, so a Daily that was five ezhuthu on Monday and six on Tuesday would throw away the only thing that makes accumulated key state worth reading. The set is 6,160 rows - 16.9 years at one a day - and its own frequency quarters are 1,540 apiece, so all three difficulty bands fill. No accept-list set is registered beside it: the Game accepts any complete row of ezhuthu, so there is nothing for one to hold.

changelog.change: Registered the missing-letters set: the anagram's serving gates with the length floor raised from 3 to 4.
changelog.why: Row 18 - a second Game is a registry entry plus a payload builder, never a rewrite of the layers above or below it, and this is the entry. Every gate is the anagram's unchanged, because what makes a word fair to be ASKED for does not depend on how it is asked: a word nobody can attest, nobody uses, or nobody can explain is a bad answer either way. The one knob that moves is minLength, and it moves because the mechanic changes what the player is given: an anagram shows every ezhuthu and asks for an order, while this shows all but one and asks which is missing, so the context a 3-ezhuthu word can offer is two letters. Measured over the 31,055-row served set, only 46.4 percent of 3-ezhuthu words have any single-blank mask that no OTHER served word also fits, against 94.8 percent at four, 99.9 at five and 100 at six - so a length floor of 4 is what turns per-blank ambiguity from the common case into the exception. wordClasses stays headword alone even though the contract offers colloquial for the recognition Games: the published lexicon holds exactly one colloquial row, so naming it would be a gesture with no rows behind it, and adding it later is a one-word edit here.

changelog.change: Added servingRules, holding the participial suffixes every set demotes and the gloss labels that mark a row as an obscenity.
changelog.why: Defect 2 - the board dealt mozhiyaana, migudhiyaana, urundaiyaana and thavaRillaadha, which are participial adjectives rather than headwords, and at rank 1,968 it dealt a surface the source itself glosses as an obscene word. Neither is reachable from the six gates: word-hood labels inflection from collected verb-form lists, so a peyareccham those lists do not contain arrives with a tier-1 listing and a clean shape, and no lexicon column says a word is coarse - the source writes that into the gloss as a usage label. The knobs hang off the REGISTRY beside denylistPath rather than off a set, because a participle is not a headword and an obscenity is not a Daily answer whichever Game is asking. Requiring the stripped stem to be an attested headword was measured and REJECTED: sandhi rewrites the stem when the suffix lands, so undoing it means guessing which spelling the writer started from, and the guess left 186 of the 1,063 matches on the board including mozhiyaana and thavaRillaadha - two of the four surfaces this rule exists to remove. The suffix ending alone, with a linking vowel and a stem floor, removed 1,063 rows of which hand inspection found none a Tamil dictionary lists as a headword. The -iya ending was measured and REJECTED at 202 rows, because indhiya, dhesiya, pudhiya, siRiya, periya, ariya and iniya are all real vocabulary.

changelog.change: Added denylistPath, naming the curated served deny-list every set is cut against.
changelog.why: Row 16 - the served set opened with Tamil's grammar and with the personal names and mastheads a news corpus makes frequent, and because frequency is a difficulty axis they landed in the EASY band, which is the band a player meets most. No selection knob can express the difference: a part-of-speech rule was measured and rejected, since pos is a union across 21 sources and appa (father) and arasu (government) both carry interjection. The path hangs off the REGISTRY rather than off a set because what makes a word unservable is true of every Game, and a per-set deny-list would let the next set opt out of it by omission.

changelog.change: Added the categories and pos selection dimensions to a set's selection, and registered the first themed set, themed-nature.
changelog.why: Row 15 of the lexicon pipeline - a themed round is the Daily's variety mechanism: three unrelated anagrams are a list, three that share a theme are a round, and that is a selection constraint rather than a new engine. A theme ships as a GROUP of categories because the single categories are tiny - the largest is a couple of hundred rows before the gates and several are under twenty - so a single-category Daily would last days rather than years. Neither dimension may gate an ordinary set: fewer than 3,000 published headwords carry a category at all, so a set that named one by accident would collapse.

changelog.change: Replaced masterPath with lexiconPath and the bands / requireValidWordFinal knobs with the four serving gates: wordClasses, minAttestations with minTier1Attestations, minFrequency and requireMeaning.
changelog.why: Row 12 of the lexicon pipeline - the set is now cut from the published lexicon, so what a word IS can gate what a player is asked to spell. The old knobs could only ask where a token ranked in a scraped corpus, which is why the committed set served a political party and a sitting politician. wordClasses is an allow-list so nothing reaches a player by omission; the tier-1 leg exists because a spellchecker wordlist agreeing with another bare list is not evidence.

changelog.change: Dropped the requireCoAnagram knob from the anagram set's selection.
changelog.why: Row 1 of the lexicon pipeline - a scramble of a word with no second arrangement is an ordinary puzzle, while demanding a partner cut the served set 106-fold and selected for bound stems, because fragments are what collide with real words. The multiset index now records anagramFanOut on each row instead of deciding admission.

changelog.change: Turned on requireValidWordFinal for the anagram set.
changelog.why: Row 13 content-quality pass - the scraped corpus pairs sandhi artifacts and transliterated loanwords with each other, and a served answer must be a word a Tamil speaker recognises (Player).

changelog.change: Initial derived-wordlist registry: the anagram set, cut from the ranked master at 3-6 ezhuthu, common/mid bands, co-anagram required.
changelog.why: Row 9 - adding another Game's wordlist must be a data change plus a re-run, never a code rewrite (the corpus and the daily puzzle are different layers).

servingRules.note: The two exclusions that need no curation, because the published data already carries the signal. Both are SERVING decisions on the same terms as the deny-list: every row named here keeps its published class and its published facts and is only kept off the board. Numbers below are over the 32,122-row anagram set committed on 2026-08-19.

participialSuffixes.note: The -aana peyareccham: any noun or verb plus -aana becomes an adjective, so thevai gives thevaiyaana and azhagu gives azhagaana. 721 served rows, every one of them a participial or attributive form; the closest calls are four Sanskrit -aana borrowings whose Tamil dictionary headword carries -am (piradhaanam, vinjnjaanam). minStemEzhuthu 1 is what keeps vaan (sky) and aana on the board.

The -aadha negative peyareccham, which also swallows the -illaadha compound: 218 served rows including illaadha itself and thavaRillaadha. Every one is a negated form of a verb or a noun; none is a dictionary headword.

The -ulla possessive participle - 'having X' - as in payanulla and uyirulla: 124 served rows. The linking u is load-bearing here, not decoration: without it the pattern also matches kolla, mella and kulla, which are ordinary words. minStemEzhuthu 1 then holds the same line one ezhuthu further out.

sets.note: headword only, because the anagram asks the player to PRODUCE an exact ezhuthu sequence: a word whose spelling is unsettled hands out tiles encoding one dialect and punishes every other, and a proper noun is a person or a party rather than a puzzle answer. 3-6 ezhuthu keeps a scramble solvable on a phone in a 2-minute burst (2 tiles has one wrong arrangement, which is a coin flip). Two attestations with at least one from a dictionary rather than a bare list: a spellchecker wordlist is several times the size of the largest dictionary and co-occurs with nearly any orthographically legal string, so two bare lists agreeing says nothing. minFrequency 1 keeps out the museum piece that no living Tamil text contains, and requireMeaning keeps out the word the game could not explain once the player had solved it. Whether the tiles also spell something else is RECORDED per row as anagramFanOut rather than required: it is what lets a Game answer 'that is a word, but not today's', and as an admission test it threw away 106 words out of every 107.

The anagram's serving gates unchanged, with the length floor at 4. The gates do not move because they answer a question the mechanic does not change - is this a word a player can be asked for at all - and the floor does because the mechanic changes what the player is holding: blanking one ezhuthu of a 3-ezhuthu word leaves two letters of context, and over the served set fewer than half of those masks have a single answer, against 94.8 percent at four ezhuthu. Which ezhuthu is hidden is the GENERATOR's decision, not a selection knob: a word is admitted here on what it IS, and a mask that admits a second real word is picked around rather than filtered on, because a mask is a property of the deal and not of the word.

The anagram's serving gates unchanged, with the length pinned to exactly 6 ezhuthu at both ends. The gates do not move because they answer a question the mechanic does not change - is this a word a player can be asked for at all. The length is pinned rather than ranged because a wordle's board, its keyboard readout and its shareable grid all assume ONE width; a Daily that was five ezhuthu on Monday and six on Tuesday would throw away the only thing that makes the accumulated keyboard state worth reading. Six rather than the five the roadmap sketched, and the reason is a measurement that runs opposite to English: Tamil's alphabet is 247 ezhuthu and effectively constant across lengths, so an extra position is an extra constraint against a fixed alphabet rather than an extra degree of freedom, and the simulated median solve falls from 15 guesses at 3 ezhuthu to 10 at 4, 7 at 5 and 5 at 6. wordClasses stays headword alone on the same terms as the other two sets.

The anagram's serving gates unchanged, with the length floor at 4 and the ceiling at 6. The gates do not move because they answer a question the mechanic does not change - is this a word a player can be asked for at all. The floor moves for a reason particular to a grid: a 4-ezhuthu word is four cells, and an 8x8 board holds hundreds of straight runs that long, so a shorter word turns up in the filler about as often as it is placed on purpose - measured, an unintended served word appears on 74.2 percent of boards when 4-ezhuthu words count and on 7.7 percent when only 5 and 6 do. It is a floor rather than a rejection because an unintended word is RECORDED and answered ('that is a word, but not on today's list'), never treated as a defect. The ceiling holds at 6 because a 7-ezhuthu word fits an 8-wide grid only along a full row, column or main diagonal, and a word that can only ever be in one of those places stops being hidden. Which words share a board, and where each one lands, are the GENERATOR's decisions rather than selection knobs: a word is admitted here on what it IS.

The anagram's serving gates unchanged, narrowed to the nature theme - so every word here is also a word the ordinary set serves, and a themed day can never be easier or harder to justify than an ordinary one. The theme is a GROUP of ten categories rather than one, because one category is a few dozen rows: Birds alone would run out inside a month. The group also has to be a theme a player can PLAY - someone told the round is about nature can name five plausible candidates before seeing a tile, which is what Nouns or Verbs could never do, and it excludes 98.7 percent of the servable set, so knowing it is worth something. Nothing here is hand picked: change the categories or the aliases they normalize through and re-run the rebuild.
